title: Linear Search
description: Understand how **linear search** checks data **sequentially**, handles **found and not-found** cases, and why its runtime **grows with input size**.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
**Linear Search** is the **simplest searching algorithm**. It works by checking elements **one by one until the target is found** or the collection ends. Think of it like looking for a book on a shelf by **scanning each book from left to right** until you find the one you want.

The algorithm does not require **sorting, recursion, or extra data structures**. It uses a direct sequential scan. This makes it one of the best first examples for understanding how search algorithms work.

Despite its simplicity, linear search is used in many real-world systems, especially when data is **unsorted, small, or accessed infrequently**.

Understanding linear search builds the **foundation for learning more advanced search algorithms** like binary search.

sections.title: Why Linear Search Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems still use **sequential searching**. A program may scan attendance lists, search through unsorted files, check notifications, or find a name in a small contact list.

Linear Search matters because **not all data is sorted**. When the input has no order, there is **no safe way to skip elements**. You must inspect each candidate directly.

Another reason linear search is useful is that it works on **any data structure that supports sequential access**, like arrays and linked lists. It also **stops early** if the target is found at the beginning.

For small datasets with **less than 100 items**, linear search is often faster than more complex algorithms because it has **no setup overhead**.
bullets: It is **simple to implement and debug**.
It is practical for **small datasets or one-time searches**.

sections.title: Core Idea of Linear Search
sections.content:
Linear Search compares each array element with the **target value in order**. It starts at **index 0 and moves forward** one step at a time.

If the current element matches the target, the algorithm **returns the current index**. If the algorithm reaches the end without finding a match, it returns a **not-found value such as -1**.

Unlike Binary Search, Linear Search **does not divide the search space** or eliminate large sections. It simply **checks elements in sequence**.

This approach is **guaranteed to find the target** if it exists, but it may need to **check every element in the worst case**.

sections.title: Searching Through an Array
sections.content:
Suppose the program searches for the number 11 inside the array [3, 8, 5, 11, 2]. The algorithm compares 3 with 11, then 8 with 11, then 5 with 11. None of these match.

When the algorithm compares 11 with 11, the **target is found and the index 3 is returned**. Because the target appears before the end, the algorithm **can stop early**. It does not need to check the remaining elements.

If the program searches for a value that does not exist, like 10, **every element must be checked**. The algorithm goes through all 5 elements, **finds no match, and returns -1**.

The worst case happens when the **target is at the end or not present at all**. In both situations, the algorithm must **examine every element**.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
A correct Linear Search implementation must have **three important behaviors**. First, it must **traverse the array sequentially**. Second, it must **return immediately** when a match is found. Third, it must **clearly indicate when no match exists**.

The basic version returns the index of the **first occurrence** of the target. If the target is not found, it **returns -1**. This -1 is a **sentinel value** because array indices are never negative.

Variations include **counting how many times the target appears**, finding the **last occurrence** instead of the first, searching only within a **specific range of indices**, and **collecting all matching indices** into a list.

These variations are useful for different real-world problems. For example, counting occurrences is helpful for **frequency analysis**, while finding the last occurrence is useful when you need the **most recent match**.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Linear Search has **O(n) worst-case time complexity**. This means the algorithm may need to **inspect every element**. If you double the size of the array, the **worst-case time also doubles**.

The best case is **O(1)**, which happens when the target is the **first element**. Only one comparison is needed. The average case is also **O(n)** because on average you will **check about half of the elements**.

Space complexity is **O(1)**. The algorithm only uses a **few variables like a loop counter and the return value**. It does not create new arrays that grow with input size.

For very large arrays, linear search **becomes slow**. For n=10 million, it may take a **noticeable amount of time**. For n=1 billion, it is **impractical**. This is why binary search is preferred when the **data is sorted**.

chart.title: Linear Search growth
chart.description: Linear Search grows proportionally with input size. The chart compares O(1), O(n), and O(log n) so the sequential scan can be contrasted with constant and logarithmic behavior.

subsections.title: Best Case
subsections.content: The best case occurs when the **target appears at the very beginning** of the array. For example, searching for 8 inside [8, 3, 5, 1] requires **only one comparison**. The algorithm **returns immediately** and never looks at the rest of the array.

subsections.title: Worst Case
subsections.content: The worst case occurs when the target is at the **very end of the array or not present at all**. Searching for 10 inside [3, 8, 5, 11, 2] **checks every element** before returning -1. For an array of size n, this means **n comparisons**.

sections.title: Linear Search vs Binary Search
sections.content:
Linear Search works on **unsorted data and scans sequentially**. It is simple and flexible but **can be slow for large datasets**. Binary Search requires **sorted data** but uses a divide and conquer strategy to **eliminate half of the remaining search space** after each comparison.

For an array of 1 million items, linear search may need **up to 1 million comparisons**. Binary search needs **only about 20 comparisons**. That is **50,000 times faster**.

However, binary search **has requirements**. The data must be sorted and stored in a structure that allows random access, **like an array**. If the data is unsorted, you must sort it first, which takes **O(n log n) time**.

Linear search is better when the **array is small**, when the **data is unsorted and you only search once**, or when the data is stored in a **linked list where random access is expensive**.

subsections.title: Advantages
bullets: It is effective for **small datasets and simple checks**.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: **Repeated searches** over huge arrays become expensive.
It does not use **ordering or indexing** to skip work.
**Optimized search algorithms** are better when data is structured.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Linear Search appears in **many practical systems**. Simple mobile apps use it to **search small contact lists**. Validation systems use it to check if a user input is in a **list of valid options**.

Small configuration files are often searched linearly because they have **only a few entries**. File scanning tools **read files sequentially** and search for specific text lines.

When data arrives in real time, like **sensor readings or log entries**, the data is chronological and **not sorted**. Linear search is the **natural choice**.

Linear Search is also commonly used as a **teaching algorithm**. It clearly shows comparison flow, stopping conditions, and the **relationship between input size and runtime**.

subsections.title: Mistake: Forgetting to stop after a match
subsections.content: When the task asks for the first matching index, the algorithm should **return immediately after the first match is found**. Continuing to search would **return a later index**, which is incorrect.

subsections.title: Mistake: Returning the element instead of the index
subsections.content: Many search tasks ask for the **position of the target**, not the target value itself. Read the problem carefully. Some problems want the **index**, others want the **value**, and others want a **boolean true or false**.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring the not-found case
subsections.content: A search algorithm must define what happens when the **target does not exist**. In many beginner problems, **-1 is used** because indices are never negative. Alternatives include **returning None or raising an exception**.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Linear Search checks elements **sequentially from first to last**.
It works on **unsorted data** with no preprocessing required.
The best case is **O(1)** when the target is the first element.
The worst case is **O(n)** when the target is missing or at the end.
Linear Search is simple and reliable, but **not ideal for repeated searches** over large datasets.
